rows.evidence: unchanged since 7254468 (git diff checked); round-17 evidence: Re-derived. Boole: 1 - H(z_B) <= sum_k P(|Z_k| > z_B) = K x 2(1 - Phi(z_B)) = K x alpha/K = alpha, so H(z_B) >= 1 - alpha and h <= z_B. Independence: H(x) = (2 Phi(x) - 1)^K, so h = Phi^-1((1 + (1-alpha)^(1/K))/2). scipy (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify8-L05-L06/scripts/math_checks.py): K = 20, alpha = 0.05 gives z_B = 3.023341, (1 + 0.95^(1/20))/2 = 0.998719, h = 3.015995, i.e. 'Phi^-1(0.998719) = 3.016, against Bonferroni's 3.023' (gain 0.243%). The replacement sentence 'Apart from a small gain that exists even under independence, the gain comes from dependence' is now true and agrees with the Remark's next sentence and with Lab 4's interpretation: by quadrature over the common factor, the limiting sup-t value for equicorrelated normals is 3.0160 at rho = 0, 2.9805 at 0.3 and 2.4794 at 0.9, never above the independence value (Sidak's inequality for Gaussian vectors), so everything beyond the 0.007 gain at rho = 0 is due to dependence. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L05.html lines 596-598 (equicorrelated normals are MTP2 for 0 <= rho < 1; one-sided p-values; the Simes step at line 598), Lab 5 hypothesis (line 638)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 7254468 (git diff checked); round-17 evidence: Re-derived at d10fb51. (a) Sigma = (1-rho) I + rho 11' with Sherman-Morrison: Sigma^{-1} = (1/(1-rho)) [I - rho 11'/(1-rho+m0 rho)], so the off-diagonal entries of Q are -rho/((1-rho)(1-rho+m0 rho)) <= 0 for 0 <= rho < 1. (b) For a normal density with precision Q, log f(z) = const - (1/2) z'Qz; with u = x v y and v = x ^ y, u_i^2 + v_i^2 = x_i^2 + y_i^2, so the diagonal terms cancel and log f(u) + log f(v) - log f(x) - log f(y) = (1/2) sum_{i != j} Q_ij (x_i x_j + y_i y_j - u_i u_j - v_i v_j). The bracket is 0 when (x_i - y_i)(x_j - y_j) >= 0 and equals (x_i - y_i)(x_j - y_j) <= 0 otherwise (checked in the four sign cases), so each term Q_ij times the bracket is >= 0 and f(u) f(v) >= f(x) f(y). Numerical spot check (num/simes_mtp2_check.out): 200,000 random pairs for each of (m, rho) = (3, 0.2), (5, 0.7), (10, 0.95), (20, 0): min(lhs - rhs) = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, -1.4e-14 (rounding), violations 0. (c) One-sided p-values are decreasing in z coordinatewise, which swaps join and meet, and the Jacobian is a product of one-coordinate factors that cancels because {u_i, v_i} = {x_i, y_i}: the true-null p-values are MTP2 as the page says. PASS.

rows.evidence: unchanged since 7254468 (git diff checked); round-17 evidence: Re-derived after the notation change. Dividing every constant of (3) by c = c(floor(gamma m) + 1) is (3) at alpha' = alpha/c (linear in alpha). Theorem 7.5 at level alpha' gives P(FDP > gamma) <= P(U_{l<=M} {q_(l) <= l alpha'/m0}). Lemma 7.6 with t = m0 and beta_l = l alpha'/m0 (nondecreasing, <= alpha' <= 1 for l <= M <= m0, increments alpha'/m0) gives m0 sum_{l<=M} alpha'/(m0 l) = alpha' c(M) <= alpha' c(floor(gamma m) + 1) = alpha, because M <= floor(gamma m) + 1 and c is increasing. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L05.html Proposition 7.8 and proof (lines 600-607)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 7254468 (git diff checked); round-17 evidence: Re-derived after the rename A -> D. If the original procedure makes no false rejection, the augmented procedure rejects R = R0 + D' with D' = min(D, m - R0) <= D, at most D' of them false; R = 0 gives FDP = 0; otherwise FDP <= D'/(R0 + D') <= D/(R0 + D) because x -> x/(R0 + x) is increasing; and D <= gamma R0/(1 - gamma) iff D (1 - gamma) <= gamma R0 iff D <= gamma (R0 + D), so FDP <= gamma. Hence {FDP > gamma} needs a false rejection by the original procedure: probability <= alpha. Correct, and the letters D, D' no longer clash with the active set A.

Proposal: J_b = the min(k-1,|R_{j-1}|) strategies of R_{j-1} with the largest t*_{b,i}; e_j = the ceil((1-alpha)B)-th smallest over draws of max^{(k)} over A_j union J_b. Bound: fix a draw and an admissible I subset of R_{j-1} with |I| <= k-1; let x be the k-th largest over A_j union I; at least k statistics are >= x, n_A in A_j and n_I in I; J_b contains at least n_I of R_{j-1}'s statistics >= x (because |J_b| >= |I| and J_b are the largest), so A_j union J_b has at least k statistics >= x and its k-th largest >= x draw by draw; hence c(A_j union I) <= e_j and d_j <= e_j (quantile monotone). Control: the pathwise chain of Theorem 7.10 uses e_{j'} >= d_{j'} >= c(I_0). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L05.html line 598 (new T span: 'In this design the Simes inequality also follows from Lesson 3 alone'); Lesson 3 Definition 5.1, Theorem 5.2, Proposition 5.3 (course/modules/S/S7/L03.html lines 262-282); Theorem 7.5 (L05.html lines 559-571)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 7254468 (git diff checked); round-17 evidence: Derivation, written out and checked: (1) Lab 5's true-null statistics are z_j = sqrt(rho) W + sqrt(1-rho) eps_j with mu_j = 0 (the lab code: z = sqrt(rho) w + sqrt(1-rho) e + mu), p_j = 1 - Phi(z_j), rho in [0,1): this is Proposition 5.3's model restricted to the nulls, so the true-null p-values are PRDS on every subset (Definition 5.1). (2) Theorem 5.2's hypotheses hold for the family of the m0 true-null p-values (the family is all true nulls, so PRDS on the true nulls is PRDS on the family; each p_j is super-uniform because z_j ~ N(0,1) gives p_j ~ U(0,1); P(p_j <= u) = u > 0 for u > 0). Its bound FDR <= m0' q / m' with m' = m0' = m0 gives FDR <= q = alpha for BH at level alpha on the family. (3) When every hypothesis in the family is true, V = R, so FDR = E[1{R >= 1}] = P(R >= 1). (4) BH at level alpha on m0 p-values (step-up) rejects at least one hypothesis iff q_(l) <= l alpha/m0 for some l <= m0. Hence P(union_{l<=m0} {q_(l) <= l alpha/m0}) <= alpha: the Simes inequality for the true-null p-values. (5) Theorem 7.5 (containment {FDP > gamma} subset of union_{l<=M}{q_(l) <= l alpha/m0}, M <= m0, for the step-down with constants (3)) gives P(FDP > gamma) <= alpha for every rho in [0,1). rows.evidence: Counter-evidence search, from scratch, at 3203b7e (VERIFIER 2.3; BUILDER_RULES 5). (a) Lu, Yonggang (2025), 'Replication crisis in finance? A unified modeling framework for reconciling pessimism and optimism', Finance Research Letters 86, 108491, doi 10.1016/j.frl.2025.108491 (Crossref: published 2025-12; no abstract in Crossref; OpenAlex: no abstract; ScienceDirect not retried, the brief reports HTTP 403). The same-titled working paper, SSRN doi 10.2139/ssrn.5519818, has a Crossref JATS abstract (curl https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2139/ssrn.5519818, read this round), which says: 'can arise from different prior beliefs' and 'An empirical illustration shows that "pessimistic" versus "optimistic" conclusions reflect different points along a spectrum of prior assumptions, rather than contradictory evidence.' The published abstract may differ; this is the best text available. Assessment: the page's claim is that HLZ's 'most claimed research findings ... are likely false' is contested; Lu contests its evidential status (the pessimistic conclusion is a prior-dependent position, not contradictory evidence). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L06.html line 330 ('Exchangeability is assumed, not justified. Bonferroni, Holm and BHY treat every hypothesis alike.') and the Section 6 normal-approximation paragraph
rows.evidence: Classified at 3203b7e as definitional. 'Bonferroni, Holm and BHY treat every hypothesis alike' follows from Definition 2.1 and the step-down and step-up rules (the procedures use the p-values only through their ranks and the values of the statistics; the threshold of Bonferroni is the same at every step). 'Neither holds exactly for small samples, fat tails or serially correlated predictor returns' is a statement about the asymptotic normal approximation (Lemma 2.2 and Theorem 2.3 are asymptotic in the normal approximation; the MBF formula assumes the normal test statistic). Neither is an empirical or literature claim, so neither needs a span under the page's convention, and neither carries a number. PASS.
